content: Functional gastrointestinal disorders (FGIDs) encompass a variety of idiopathic conditions that affect different regions of the gastrointestinal tract. These disorders are not caused by structural or biochemical abnormalities but are instead characterized by chronic symptoms that cannot be explained by conventional diagnostic methods. The classification of FGIDs has been refined through the Rome process, which has established a consensus-based system for categorizing and defining these disorders. The Rome I, II, and III meetings, organized by the Rome Coordinating Committee, have progressively developed this classification system and associated terminology. Functional esophageal disorders include conditions such as functional heartburn, functional chest pain of presumed esophageal origin, functional dysphagia, and globus pharyngis. These disorders are characterized by symptoms related to the esophagus without identifiable structural or biochemical causes. Functional colonic diseases, also referred to as functional bowel disorders, are a group of conditions marked by chronic abdominal complaints, such as pain or discomfort, in the absence of structural or biochemical abnormalities. Examples include functional constipation and functional rectal pain. Other FGIDs include functional dyspepsia, noncardiac chest pain, chronic functional abdominal pain, and irritable bowel syndrome (IBS). These conditions often present with a range of symptoms, including pain, altered bowel habits, and discomfort, which can significantly impact a patient’s quality of life. Epidemiological studies have shown that FGIDs are highly prevalent, affecting approximately 60-70% of the populations in Canada and the United States. This highlights the significant burden of these disorders on healthcare systems and the need for effective management strategies.
